documents.title: READING CHECK: “EVERY AFTERNOON” AND “THE REEF THAT GREW BACK”
documents.directions: Read the story and the article. Then answer each question in complete sentences. When you cite, put the paragraph number in brackets, like [3].

passages.title: Every Afternoon
paragraphs: Since the moving truck took the Parks' furniture away in August, Dev had spent most afternoons on his front steps, reading the same three comic books. Across the street, Mrs. Amsel's curtain moved now and then.

On a Monday in October, she crossed the street with a key on a green ribbon. “I'm visiting my sister until Saturday,” she said. “My plant needs someone every day, right after school. Can you do that?” Dev said yes before she finished asking. That night he put the key on his own ring and checked his pocket for it twice before dinner.

Her instructions filled a whole page: half a cup of water each day, and “sit in the green chair for twenty minutes while the soil settles.” Beside it lay four envelopes, one for each day until Friday, and a chessboard with one white pawn pushed forward. A note said, “Black moves next. My moves are in the envelopes.”
The plant was a fat jade in a blue pot. Dev watered it, sat in the green chair and moved a black pawn. Playing against an envelope felt silly. He did it anyway.
On Tuesday the envelope said, “Knight to f3. The cookies in the tin are for the plant's helper.” Dev ate two and studied the board until the twenty minutes had turned into forty.

On Thursday he noticed a tag deep in the soil: “Jade. Water every two to three weeks. Do not overwater.” Dev stood holding the measuring cup. A photo on the shelf showed Mrs. Amsel, much younger, beside the same plant in the same blue pot. “She must have forgotten,” he told himself. He poured the water into the sink, then sat down and opened Thursday's envelope.
On Saturday, Dev was waiting on Mrs. Amsel's porch when her car pulled in. “How did my plant behave?” she asked.

“Fine,” Dev said. “It didn't need me much.” He handed her the key. Then he set a fifth envelope, marked Monday, on the chessboard. Mrs. Amsel looked at it for a long moment. Then she put the key back in his hand.

passages.title: The Reef That Grew Back
paragraphs: Off the northeast coast of New Zealand, about an hour's drive north of the city of Auckland, is a rocky shore near Goat Island. In 1975 it became part of the country's first marine reserve. Inside the reserve, no one may fish, gather shellfish or take anything at all.

Before then, divers there often swam over what scientists call kina barrens. Kina are spiny sea urchins. Where they crowded the rocks, they grazed every young seaweed down to bare stone. Wide patches of reef that could have held tall kelp held almost nothing but kina.

Kina have enemies. Snapper, a fish that people love to catch, crunch them up. So do spiny lobsters, which New Zealanders call crayfish. For many years, though, fishers had taken most of the big snapper and lobsters along this coast.

After the reserve began, nothing changed quickly. The snapper and lobsters that had escaped hooks and traps stayed, grew and had young. A small lobster can do little to a full-grown kina with its hard shell and spines. A large one can. Year after year, the predators inside the reserve grew bigger and more common.

Slowly, the kina became harder to find. By the late 1990s, about twenty years after fishing stopped, much of the bare rock was covered again by a thick stand of kelp. Small fish hid among the long brown blades.

One easy guess is that the water simply got cleaner. But reefs just outside the reserve are washed by the same ocean. On those reefs, where fishing went on, many of the barrens stayed. The difference between the two places was not the water. It was whether people could take the fish and lobsters.

No one planted a single strand of kelp at Goat Island. People stopped taking the animals that eat kina, and then they waited. Since the 2000s, fishing along the reserve's edges has thinned the lobsters again, and in 2025 the reserve was made larger.

sections.heading: STORY: “EVERY AFTERNOON” (Questions 1–3)
sections.directions: Answer in complete sentences. Each answer needs your idea plus a quote or exact detail from the passage, with its paragraph number.

questions.skill: infer a character's feeling and cite it

prompt.A: In paragraph 2, how does Dev feel about being asked to do the job? Name the feeling. Then quote one sentence from paragraph 2 that shows it.
prompt.B: In paragraph 5, how does Dev feel about the chess game now? Name the feeling. Then quote the sentence from paragraph 5 that shows it best.

answer.A: Dev is eager and glad to have the job. Evidence: “Dev said yes before she finished asking.” [2] (also full credit: “That night he put the key on his own ring and checked his pocket for it twice before dinner.” [2])
answer.B: Dev is interested in the game and enjoying it; he is pulled into it. Evidence: “Dev ate two and studied the board until the twenty minutes had turned into forty.” [5]

accept: A: eager, excited, glad, happy, proud, or careful/serious about the job, with a quote from [2] that shows it
B: interested, hooked, curious, enjoying it, into it, wants to win, with the sentence about the twenty minutes turning into forty [5]

why.A: He answers before the question is even finished, and he treats the key like his own and keeps checking for it: he wants this job. A student who writes 'nervous' and quotes the pocket check gets full credit if they explain he is worried about losing the key; 'nervous' with no quote gets 1.
why.B: In [4] the game 'felt silly'; by [5] he stays twice as long as the instructions ask, thinking about the board. A student who says he still feels silly is contradicted by [5]; that is a 0 claim.

full.A: A feeling (eager, excited, glad, proud, or careful about the key) plus one of the two sentences from [2] quoted.
full.B: A feeling of interest or enjoyment plus the twenty-minutes-into-forty sentence from [5].

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

prompt.A: Why does Dev stay at Mrs. Amsel's house longer than her instructions say? Give the reason and quote the words that show it, with the paragraph number.
prompt.B: On Thursday, Dev decides something about Mrs. Amsel's instructions. What does he decide, and what detail in the same paragraph shows he is wrong? Quote the words from the story.

answer.A: He stays because he is caught up in the chess game with Mrs. Amsel (and enjoys the cookies left for him), not because the plant needs him. He “studied the board until the twenty minutes had turned into forty.” [5] Also full credit: on Thursday he still “sat down and opened Thursday's envelope” after deciding not to water [6].
answer.B: Dev decides she made a mistake: “She must have forgotten” that a jade needs very little water [6]. He is wrong because the photo shows “Mrs. Amsel, much younger, beside the same plant in the same blue pot” [6]. She has kept this plant alive for years, so she knows how to care for it; the daily watering was on purpose.

accept: A: to keep playing / think about the chess game, with the twenty-minutes-into-forty words from [5] or the words about sitting down and opening Thursday's envelope from [6]

B: he decides she forgot / made a mistake about the watering, or he decides not to water it / that the watering instruction is a mistake; he is wrong because the photo shows she has had the same plant for years (quoting the photo words from [6])

why.A: The instructions say twenty minutes [3]; in [5] he studies the board for forty. The reason is the game, not the plant: in [6] he stops watering but still opens the envelope.
why.B: Inference: Dev's conclusion in [6] is 'She must have forgotten.' The photo in the same paragraph shows her, much younger, with the same plant in the same pot, so she has cared for it for years and could not have forgotten what it needs. 'He decides she is lazy' or 'he decides the plant is sick' has no line in [6] behind it.

full.A: The reason (the chess game or the envelopes) plus the words from [5] or [6] quoted or named exactly.
full.B: His conclusion (she forgot / made a mistake, or not to water it because the instruction is a mistake) plus why it is wrong, with the photo detail from [6] quoted or named exactly (younger Mrs. Amsel, same plant, same blue pot).

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

prompt.A: At the end of the story, Mrs. Amsel puts the key back in Dev's hand. What does she mean by this? Use one detail from paragraph 8 and one detail from earlier in the story.
prompt.B: Reread paragraph 8. What does Dev's last action show he wants? Explain how it connects to something Mrs. Amsel did earlier in the story. Name exactly what she did and give that paragraph number.

answer.A: She is saying yes: Dev should keep coming over, even though she is home now. Dev has just asked to keep playing by leaving a fifth envelope marked Monday [8], copying her own envelopes from [3]. The plant was never the real reason for the visits: the tag says it needs water only every few weeks, and the photo shows she has kept the same plant for years [6], so she knew that all along. Also full credit as the earlier detail: the cookies “for the plant's helper” [5] or her curtain moving while Dev sat alone [1].
answer.B: He wants the visits and the chess game with Mrs. Amsel to go on after the plant job is over. He leaves a fifth envelope marked Monday [8], the same way she left envelopes with her moves for each day [3]. Now he is the one inviting her to keep playing.

accept: A: she wants him to keep visiting / keep playing chess with her; she accepts his invitation, with the Monday envelope [8] and one earlier detail: her envelopes [3], the tag or photo [6], the cookies “for the plant's helper” [5], or her curtain moving while Dev sat alone [1]
B: he wants to keep playing chess / keep visiting her, connected to her envelope game: the day-by-day envelopes in [3] or the Tuesday envelope with her move in [5]

why.A: Second step: the student has to connect Dev's Monday envelope [8] to her envelopes [3], and see from [6] (the tag and the old photo) that the key was never about the plant. 'She trusts him with her house' is the story type's default reading; it misses that the plant doesn't need daily care and that she is answering his envelope.
why.B: Second step: the student must connect his Monday envelope [8] to her envelopes in [3]. 'He wants to keep the key' or 'he wants to be paid' is ruled out: he hands the key back first [8], and nothing in the story mentions pay.

full.A: She wants him to keep coming / accepts his invitation, with the Monday envelope from [8] and one earlier detail named exactly ([3] envelopes, [6] tag/photo, [5] cookies for the plant's helper, or [1] her curtain moving).
full.B: He wants the game/visits to continue, with the Monday envelope [8] linked to her envelopes, named exactly ([3] the envelopes for each day, or [5] the Tuesday envelope with her move).

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

sections.heading: ARTICLE: “THE REEF THAT GREW BACK” (Questions 4–6)
sections.directions: Answer in complete sentences. Each answer needs your idea plus a quote or exact detail from the passage, with its paragraph number.

prompt.A: What does the word blades mean in paragraph 5? Write the meaning. Then copy the words from paragraph 5 that helped you figure it out.
prompt.B: What does the word stand mean in paragraph 5? Write the meaning. Then copy the words from paragraph 5 that helped you figure it out.

answer.A: Here blades are the long, flat, leaf-like parts of the kelp, not the sharp edge of a knife. Clues: “a thick stand of kelp” and “Small fish hid among the long brown blades” [5].
answer.B: A stand is a group of plants (here kelp) growing close together in one place. Clues: “covered again by a thick stand of kelp” and “Small fish hid among the long brown blades” [5].

accept: A: the leaves of the kelp, or its long flat leaves / leaf-like parts / strips / parts (seaweed), with a clue copied from [5] (for example “thick stand of kelp” or “Small fish hid among the long brown blades”)
B: a group / patch / bunch of plants (kelp) growing together, with a clue copied from [5]

why.A: Not the everyday sense (the cutting edge of a knife or a skate). In [5] the blades belong to the 'stand of kelp' and are 'long' and 'brown', and fish 'hid among' them: they are the kelp's long, flat leaves. 'Something sharp' is ruled out: small fish hide among them.
why.B: Not the everyday sense (to stand up, or a table or booth). In [5] the stand 'covered' the rock and fish 'hid among' its blades: a crowd of kelp growing together.

full.A: A meaning like 'the long, flat leaves of the kelp' plus a clue copied from [5].
full.B: A meaning like 'a group of kelp growing close together' plus a clue copied from [5].

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

prompt.A: Fishing stopped at Goat Island in 1975, but the kelp did not come back for many years. According to this article, why did it take so long? Copy the words from the article that explain it.
prompt.B: According to this article, why did many reefs just outside the reserve stay bare? Explain the steps. Copy the article's words for at least one step.

answer.A: The lobsters that were left were still small, and small ones cannot hurt a grown kina, so the kina were not eaten until the lobsters grew large, which took years. “A small lobster can do little to a full-grown kina with its hard shell and spines. A large one can.” [4]
answer.B: Outside the reserve, “where fishing went on, many of the barrens stayed” [6]. Fishers kept taking the big snapper and lobsters [3], so there were few predators to eat the kina, and the kina kept grazing the young seaweed down to bare stone [2]. It was not the water: those reefs “are washed by the same ocean” [6].

accept: A: the lobsters had to grow from small to large before they could eat grown kina, with the small-lobster / large-lobster words from [4] copied (“A small lobster can do little to a full-grown kina” or “A large one can”); also full credit: the predators had to grow bigger and more common, with “Year after year, the predators inside the reserve grew bigger and more common” [4] copied

B: fishing continued there, so few predators, so many kina, so the kina ate the seaweed, with at least one step's words copied from the article: “where fishing went on, many of the barrens stayed” [6], “are washed by the same ocean” [6], “fishers had taken most of the big snapper and lobsters” [3], or “grazed every young seaweed down to bare stone” [2] (not the [7] line about the reserve's edges: it is about recent years, not why the outside reefs stayed bare)

why.A: Only this article gives the size detail: [4] says a small lobster 'can do little to a full-grown kina' and 'A large one can,' and the predators grew 'year after year.' A reader who knows the usual predator-urchin-kelp story but not this article can give the reason but not the words (1 point at most). 'The kelp grows slowly' is not what this article says.
why.B: The article never says the whole chain in one place: [6] says the barrens stayed where fishing went on and the ocean is the same, [3] that fishers took the big predators, [2] what kina do to seaweed. A reader who knows the textbook story can give the chain but not the article's words (1 point at most). 'The water was dirtier there' is ruled out by [6] (same ocean).

full.A: The lobsters had to grow large before they could eat grown kina, plus the small-vs-large lobster words from [4] copied; or the predators had to grow bigger and more common, plus “Year after year, the predators inside the reserve grew bigger and more common” [4] copied. The general idea ('the predators had to come back') with no copied words earns 1.
full.B: The chain fishing → few predators → many kina → no kelp, plus at least one step in the article's own words, copied. Paragraph numbers alone earn 1.

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

questions.skill: infer the author's purpose and reasoning

prompt.A: Paragraph 6 brings up an idea and then argues against it. What is the idea? Copy the exact words the author uses to show it is wrong. Then explain what this proves about why the kelp came back.
prompt.B: Paragraph 7 says that people “waited.” Use paragraph 4 to explain why waiting was needed. Then explain what this shows about how the kelp came back. Quote the words you use.

answer.A: The idea is that the water got cleaner. The author answers that reefs just outside the reserve “are washed by the same ocean,” yet many barrens stayed there [6]. Since the water is the same, the difference must be the fishing rule: inside, the predators were left alone, so they ate the kina and the kelp grew back.
answer.B: Waiting was needed because the snapper and lobsters left after fishing stopped had to grow: “A small lobster can do little to a full-grown kina with its hard shell and spines. A large one can.” and “Year after year, the predators inside the reserve grew bigger and more common.” [4] This shows the kelp came back slowly and without people doing anything to it (“No one planted a single strand of kelp” [7]): it returned only after the predators grew big enough to eat the kina.

accept: A: the idea that cleaner water caused it, plus the author's words from [6] copied (“reefs just outside the reserve are washed by the same ocean”, with or without “where fishing went on, many of the barrens stayed”), so protecting the predators (no fishing) made the difference

B: the predators had to grow large / become more common before they could eat the grown kina, quoting [4] (the small-vs-large lobster lines or “Year after year, the predators inside the reserve grew bigger and more common”), and so the kelp came back slowly, on its own, once the predators grew, not because people planted it

why.A: Two steps: name the rejected idea, then copy the author's own evidence from [6] (the outside reefs are 'washed by the same ocean') and explain how it works as a comparison. A reader who knows reserve science can say 'the water changed' and 'reefs outside stayed bare' without reading, but not the author's words, so that earns 1 point at most. 'The author proves the ocean is polluted' is ruled out: [6] says nothing about pollution.
why.B: Two steps: connect the waiting in [7] to the growth of the predators in [4] (small lobsters can do little to grown kina), then say what that shows about the recovery (slow, by itself, through the predators). 'They waited for the water to get cleaner' is ruled out by [6] (same ocean); 'they waited for planted kelp to grow' is ruled out by [7] (no one planted any).

full.A: Names the cleaner-water idea, copies the author's words from [6] (“washed by the same ocean”), and says the fishing rule (predators) is the real cause. The general argument (the outside reefs have the same water but stayed bare) without the copied words earns 1.
full.B: Why waiting was needed (the predators had to grow big and common enough to eat grown kina) with words quoted from [4], plus what it shows (the kelp came back slowly and on its own, through the predators).

credit.partial: 1 point: a reasonable claim with no quote or exact detail from the passage, or with only a paragraph number. A paragraph number is extra, never enough on its own; a guess a reader could make without the passage earns no more than this.
notes: 0 points: no claim, or a claim the passage contradicts.

sections.heading: CONSTRUCTED RESPONSE (4 points)
sections.directions: Answer on the lines. Staple your RACE checklist to this page.

questions.skill: constructed response (RACE): infer and cite two pieces of evidence

prompt.A:
How does Dev change from the beginning of “Every Afternoon” to the end? Use RACE:
R - Restate the question.   A - Answer it.   C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers].   E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.
prompt.B:
Why did Mrs. Amsel ask Dev to come to her house every day? Use RACE:
R - Restate the question.   A - Answer it.   C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers].   E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.

answer.A: Dev changes from a boy who spends his afternoons alone to a boy who goes out of his way to keep a new friendship going. At the beginning, he sits by himself on his front steps “reading the same three comic books” [1] after the Parks move away. By the end, he waits on Mrs. Amsel's porch [7] and sets a fifth envelope marked Monday on the chessboard [8]. The first detail shows he had nothing to do and no one to do it with. The envelope shows he now wants the game to continue and is the one asking for it, the way Mrs. Amsel asked him with her envelopes.
answer.B: Mrs. Amsel asked Dev to come every day because she wanted to give him company and something to look forward to, not because her plant needed it. She asks him to come “every day, right after school” [2], but the tag says the jade needs water only “every two to three weeks” [6], and the old photo shows she has kept it for years [6], so she knew. She also set up a chair for twenty minutes and a chess game with a move for each day [3]. Since her curtain moved while Dev sat alone after the Parks left [1], she had noticed he was lonely and made a reason for him to visit.

why.A: Strong answers go past 'he becomes responsible' (the story type's default): the plant needed little care [6], and what changes is that Dev goes from alone [1] to inviting [8].
why.B: Strong answers use the gap between the daily visits [2]/[3] and what the plant needs [6], plus her watching [1]. 'She didn't know how to care for plants' is ruled out by the photo [6]; 'she wanted to test if he was responsible' has no line behind it.

credit.full: Score with the RACE checklist (Restate, Answer, Cite, Explain; 4 points each row, averaged and rounded up). Cap: if the response cites no real line or detail from the story (only invented quotes, wrong details, or bare paragraph numbers), the whole response scores at most 2 of 4, however strong Restate and Answer are.
credit.partial: An answer with no real line or detail from the story scores at most 2 of 4 in total (the cap above), and no higher than 1 on Cite. A paragraph number with no quote or exact detail is not evidence.
notes: Any two pieces of evidence that support the answer count; the model answer lists the strongest.

rubric.title: RACE CHECKLIST (staple this to your constructed response)

criteria.name: Restate
levels: I turned the question into my first sentence.
I restated part of the question.
I copied the question word for word.

criteria.name: Answer
levels: I answered every part of the question, and my answer fits all the clues in the story.
I answered the question, but my answer only fits some of the clues.
My answer is a guess or only partly answers the question.
I did not answer the question.

criteria.name: Cite
levels: Two quotes or exact details, each with a [paragraph number], and each one proves my answer.
Two pieces of evidence, but one is missing its [paragraph number] or only mentions the topic.
No real evidence from the text (made-up quotes or only paragraph numbers count as none).

criteria.name: Explain
levels: For each piece of evidence, I explained how it proves my answer (“This shows ___, so ___”).
I explained one piece of evidence.
I repeated the quote instead of explaining it.

rubric.note: Score: Add the four rows and divide by 4. I round up. Big rule: if I did not use a real quote or exact detail from the story, my whole score can be no higher than 2, even if my other rows are great. A paragraph number by itself is not evidence. Check yourself: if you showed someone only your quote, would they agree with your answer?

findings.where: Article [1] (both versions); A q5 prompt ("Fishing stopped at Goat Island in 1975")
findings.what: 1975 is right: Cape Rodney–Okakari Point (Goat Island) Marine Reserve is New Zealand's first marine reserve, set up in 1975 as a no-take reserve. 'No one may fish, gather shellfish or take anything at all' matches no-take status. Some sources give 1977 as the year it formally opened, but 1975 is the standard date (the reserve marked its 50th anniversary in 2025). A q5 repeats the same date, so the same KEEP applies there.
findings.source: reference: University of Auckland news, 'A living lab – NZ's first marine reserve turns 50' (20 Oct 2025), https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/news/2025/10/20/a-living-lab-nzs-first-marine-reserve-turns-50.html; The Conversation (Pilditch & Thrush), 'NZ's first marine reserve is turning 50', https://www.inkl.com/news/nz-s-first-marine-reserve-is-turning-50-the-lessons-from-its-recovery-are-invaluable

findings.where: Article [1]: 'Off the northeast coast of New Zealand, about an hour's drive north of the city of Auckland'
findings.what: The reserve is at Leigh, on the east coast of the upper North Island, about 90 km (roughly an hour's drive) north of Auckland. 'Northeast coast of New Zealand' is a fair description for grade 7.
findings.source: reference: University of Auckland (Leigh Marine Laboratory sits beside the reserve), link above; Department of Conservation reserve page (Goat Island / Cape Rodney–Okakari Point)

findings.where: Article [2]: kina barrens before protection; kina are spiny sea urchins that graze seaweed down to bare rock
findings.what: Correct. Kina (Evechinus chloroticus) are sea urchins. Before protection, they had made barrens, rock grazed clean of seaweed. One small point: the first full surveys were made in the late 1970s, just after the reserve began (barrens covered about 40% of the reef then). 'Before then, divers … often swam over' is still a fair statement.
findings.source: reference: Gulf Journal (Hauraki Gulf Forum), kina barrens and trophic cascades, citing Babcock et al. 1999 and Shears & Babcock 2003, https://gulfjournal.org.nz/?p=4992

findings.where: Article [3]: snapper and spiny lobsters ('crayfish') eat kina; fishing had removed most of the big ones
findings.what: Correct, and this is the predator link reported for the reserve. New Zealanders do call spiny lobster (Jasus edwardsii) 'crayfish' or 'cray'. Snapper are a heavily fished recreational species.
findings.source: reference: Gulf Journal (link above); NZ Geographic, 'A tragedy of the commons', https://www.nzgeo.com/stories/a-tragedy-of-the-commons/

findings.where: Article [4]: recovery was slow; only large lobsters can handle full-grown kina; predators grew bigger and more common
findings.what: Supported. Inside the reserve, crayfish increased about four-fold by the 1990s and grew larger. Studies report that big predators take adult kina more effectively, which matches the size point the article makes in [4].
findings.source: reference: NZ Geographic (link above); Auckland Council OurAuckland, 'Goat Island… not what it used to be' (Feb 2016), https://ourauckland.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/news/2016/02/goat-island-not-what-it-used-to-be/

findings.where: Article [5]: 'By the late 1990s, about twenty years after fishing stopped, much of the bare rock was covered again by … kelp'
findings.what: Supported by Babcock et al. 1999, which reported that barrens inside the reserve had shrunk greatly and kelp (Ecklonia) had returned by about 1998. One popular account says 'about 30 years' for the full effect. 'Much of' and 'about twenty years' are a fair middle ground and avoid a percentage, as the maker intended.
findings.source: reference: Babcock, Kelly, Shears, Walker & Willis (1999), 'Changes in community structure in temperate marine reserves', Marine Ecology Progress Series 189:125–134, as summarised by Gulf Journal (link above)

findings.where: Article [6]: reefs just outside the reserve, where fishing went on, kept many barrens; the difference was fishing, not the water
findings.what: Supported. Fished reefs next to the reserve stayed dominated by kina barrens, and the inside/outside comparison is the main evidence scientists used. B q5 (why reefs outside stayed bare) has a factually sound answer. See the next finding for the minority view.
findings.source: reference: Babcock et al. 1999; Auckland Council 2016 (link above): 'Unprotected areas outside the marine reserve are dominated by kina barrens because of a lack of predators'

findings.where: Article [6]–[7], and A q6 / B q6 (the cause the article argues for, and the questions that ask students to explain it)
findings.what: The article presents 'fishing stopped → predators returned → kina fell → kelp grew back' as settled fact. This is the mainstream scientific account (Babcock, Shears). A known minority view, led by local diver and naturalist Floor Anthoni, calls it 'the snapper–urchin–kelp myth' and points to other causes such as urchin disease and recruitment. Simplifying to the mainstream view is normal for grade 7 and does not make any key false.
findings.source: reference: Babcock et al. 1999 (mainstream); Seafriends, 'The snapper–urchin–kelp myth', https://seafriends.org.nz/indepth/snapper-urchin.htm (dissent)

judgment.issue: The article says protecting predators is what brought the kelp back. Most scientists agree, but a few dispute it.
options: Keep it as it is (the mainstream scientific explanation, fine for grade 7)
Soften paragraph 6 a little, e.g. 'Scientists who compared the two places concluded the difference was…'
judgment.why: The mainstream view is well supported, and q6 is about following the author's argument.

findings.where: Article as a whole (title 'The Reef That Grew Back', ending [7]); also teacher notes or 'why' lines that describe the reserve today
findings.what: The story is told in the past tense and is true as history. Since the 2000s, though, crayfish inside the reserve have dropped to below their 1975 level and to less than a quarter of their 1990s peak. Fish are less plentiful than in the late 1970s, and scientists blame fishing at the reserve's edges. Kina barrens have expanded again. In 2025 the Hauraki Gulf Marine Protection Act made the reserve about four times larger. Nothing in the article says 'still', so nothing is false, but a reader could take the ending as a permanent result. Sweep: I found no present-tense claim about today's reef in the student copy. If pack.json `why` lines or notes say the reef 'is' kelp forest now, that place needs a FIX.
findings.source: reference: Auckland Council OurAuckland 2016 (link above); NZ Geographic, 'A tragedy of the commons' (link above); University of Auckland 2025 (link above); The Conversation 2025 (link above)

judgment.issue: The reef grew back in the 1990s, but in recent years crayfish have declined and some barrens have returned. The article doesn't say so.
options: Keep it as it is (the article is about what happened by the late 1990s, and it is accurate for that period)

Add one closing sentence, e.g. 'Since then, fishing along the reserve's edges has thinned the lobsters again, and in 2025 the reserve was made larger.' Facts to check: crayfish decline since the 2000s (Auckland Council 2016, Shears); 2025 enlargement under the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act (boundary to about 3 km, roughly four times larger).
judgment.why: Pet World's content rule asks for facts to be current. One sentence fixes this and keeps the paragraph numbers that the questions cite. Adding it to the end of [7] keeps it at 7 paragraphs. It would add about 25 words.

findings.where: Article [7]: 'No one planted a single strand of kelp at Goat Island'
findings.what: True for the recovery described (natural recovery, no replanting). The kina-removal trials in the Gulf from the 2020s were later and took place mostly elsewhere, and they did not plant kelp.
findings.source: reference: Gulf Journal, 'Removing kina from barrens helps kelp recover but is not a solution on its own' (Apr 2024), https://gulfjournal.org.nz/2024/04/removing-kina-from-barrens-helps-kelp-recover-but-is-not-a-solution-on-its-own/

findings.where: Story 'Every Afternoon' [6]: jade tag 'Water every two to three weeks. Do not overwater.'
findings.what: Correct. Jade (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that is watered only when the soil dries out, roughly every 2–3 weeks. Daily half-cups would overwater it, which is the clue the plot depends on. Jade plants are long-lived, so the old photo with the same plant is plausible.
findings.source: reference: standard houseplant care guidance (e.g. university extension houseplant sheets on Crassula ovata)

findings.where: Story [3]–[5]: the chess setup (white pawn already moved, black moves next, Tuesday envelope 'Knight to f3')
findings.what: Legal and consistent. White opened with a pawn move, Dev replied as Black, and Nf3 is a legal second move for White from the starting position in standard algebraic notation. The calendar also adds up: the reply is made Monday, the four envelopes cover Tuesday to Friday, she returns Saturday, and the fifth envelope is 'Monday'.
findings.source: reference: FIDE Laws of Chess, Appendix C (algebraic notation)

findings.where: Article [7], new closing sentence: 'in 2025 the reserve was made about four times larger' (same passage text shown with A q4–q7 and B q4–q7); also the B q5 key if it quotes this line
findings.what: The year is right: the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act passed on 8 October 2025 and took effect on 25 October 2025, extending the Cape Rodney–Okakari Point (Goat Island) reserve (the offshore boundary moves from about 800 m to about 3 km). The size is not settled: the Department of Conservation's own reserve page says the reserve 'will triple in size', while University of Auckland / The Conversation pieces say 'about four times larger' or 'quadruple', and an earlier DOC page said 'nearly quadruple'. The gap likely comes from 'adds three times its area' vs 'ends up four times its area', and 'four times larger' is itself ambiguous. A number students may quote should not depend on that. Suggested wording (direction, keeps the sentence and paragraph count): 'Since then, fishing along the reserve's edges has thinned the lobsters again, and in 2025 the reserve was made much larger.' Facts to check: 2025 extension in force (DOC, Gazette 2025-ln6286). If the maker prefers a number, use DOC's 'about three times larger' and cite DOC.
findings.source: reference: DOC, 'Maps and boundaries for Cape Rodney-Okakari Point Marine Reserve' (says it will triple in size from 25 Oct 2025), https://www.doc.govt.nz/parks-and-recreation/places-to-go/auckland/places/cape-rodney-okakari-point-marine-reserve-goat-island/map-and-boundaries/; NZ Gazette notice 2025-ln6286 (Cape Rodney–Okakari Point Extension Marine Reserve, commencement 25 Oct 2025), https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2025-ln6286; Scoop, 'Marine Conservation Milestone Celebrated At Te Hawere-A-Maki' (Oct 2025, 'tripled'), https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/AK2510/S00962.htm; University of Auckland, 'A living lab – NZ's first marine reserve turns 50' (20 Oct 2025, 'about four times larger', 800 m to 3 km), https://www.auckland.ac.nz/en/news/2025/10/20/a-living-lab-nzs-first-marine-reserve-turns-50.html

findings.where: Article [7], new closing sentence: 'Since then, fishing along the reserve's edges has thinned the lobsters again'
findings.what: Supported. Monitoring reported crayfish (and snapper) inside the reserve below their 1975 level and under a quarter of their 1990s peak, with the decline continuing afterward. Dr Nick Shears (University of Auckland) attributes it mainly to cray pots set at the reserve's 800 m boundary, where crayfish move out to feed on the sand flats. 'Since then' (after the late-1990s recovery) matches the timing. This also settles round 1's second JUDGMENT (article not current): fixed.
findings.source: reference: Auckland Council OurAuckland, 'Goat Island… not what it used to be' (Feb 2016), https://ourauckland.aucklandcouncil.govt.nz/news/2016/02/goat-island-not-what-it-used-to-be/; RNZ, 'Crayfish, snapper numbers drop at Goat Island reserve' (25 Feb 2016), https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regional/297393/crayfish,-snapper-numbers-drop-at-goat-island-reserve; Gulf Journal, 'Crayfish decline further', https://gulfjournal.org.nz/article/crayfish-decline-further/

findings.where: A q4 key (from CHANGES.md): 'blades' in [5] means 'the kelp's long flat leaves'
findings.what: 'Blade' is the correct term for kelp, and the context 'long brown blades' supports the meaning. But kelp is a seaweed (an alga), not a plant, and it has no true leaves; its blades are leaf-like. Calling them 'leaves' is a common simplification, and many grade 7 teachers accept it. The key should still accept 'leaves'.
findings.source: reference: NOAA Ocean Service, 'What is kelp?' (kelp has a holdfast, stipe and leaf-like blades), https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/kelp.html

judgment.issue: The answer key says kelp 'blades' are leaves. Kelp is a seaweed, so its blades are leaf-like but not true leaves.

Change the key to 'the kelp's long, flat, leaf-like parts' and still accept 'leaves' from students
judgment.why: It's a two-word change, it keeps the science accurate, and students lose nothing.

notes: Order pp-2026-11-12-g7-ela3 is a sample order for a made-up teacher: a grade 7 ELA reading quiz on inference and citing evidence, two original passages, 7 items in versions A and B, and a 4-point RACE checklist.
The work took 3 rounds and 17 agent sessions: 3 maker rounds, 8 no-passage probe runs, 3 blind tester sessions (two phases, then a recheck) and 3 fact checks.
Round 1: the maker wrote the story 'Every Afternoon' (350 words), the article 'The Reef That Grew Back' (306 words), 7 items per version and the RACE checklist.

Round 1 no-passage gate: both versions failed. With no passage, a probe earned 8 of 16 points on A, with full credit on A q5. B q5 also earned full credit from general reef knowledge and a guessed paragraph number.

Round 1 blind tester: with the passages but without the key, it agreed with the key on 12 of 12 short answers, and both RACE answers fit the model. The scoring script showed 0 of 12 because it compares free text word for word, so the match was judged by hand.

Round 1 blind tester, no-passage phase: 3 of 7 A items and 2 of 7 B items matched without the passages. This phase was shown both versions at once, against the one-version rule, so cues leaked across versions. That slip was logged as a FIX.
